place.zh: 石坳村 · 你家 · 傍晚

setup.zh: 马三踹开柴门：还差一张鹿皮、二十斤肉，入冬前交不上，墙上那张弓就归他。马小宝要你学狗叫。
setup.en: Ma San kicks the gate open: a deer hide and twenty jin of meat still owed; not paid by winter, the bow on the wall is his. Ma Xiaobao wants you to bark like a dog.

recap.zh: 马三来收租：还差一张鹿皮、二十斤肉，不然拿走爷爷的弓；马小宝推了你一把，碗碎了。
recap.en: Ma San came for the rent — a deer hide and twenty jin of meat, or grandfather's bow; Ma Xiaobao shoved you and a bowl broke.

zh: 马三来了，一脚踹开柴门。
他的目光，落在墙上那张旧弓上。
en: Ma San comes, and kicks the gate open.
"Still short a deer hide and twenty jin of meat."
His eyes settle on the old bow on the wall.

label.en: The old bow on the wall

text.zh: 弓背裂过两回，拿牛筋一圈一圈缠着，是爷爷传下来的；马三的眼睛，已在它上头停了两回。
text.en: The bow-back has split twice and is bound round and round with ox sinew — your grandfather's. Ma San's eyes have come to rest on it twice already.

text.zh: 灶台上四只碗，三只缺口，只一只是囫囵的，偏偏搁在最边上。
text.en: Four bowls on the stove: three chipped, one whole — and the whole one sits right on the edge.

text.zh: 短棍包着铁皮，棍头磨得发亮；这根棍子打过的人，只怕比你认得的人还多。
text.en: The club is sheathed in iron, its head rubbed bright. It has likely struck more people than you have ever met.

story.zh:
收租的，是马三。

马三是马家老爷的远房侄子，长得跟一扇门似的。不是像门，他本人比你家那扇门还像门——你家的门，至少还有缝。他进屋要侧着身子，侧着身子还要低头，低着头还要吸气。

他腰里别一根包了铁皮的短棍。那根棍子在石坳村比他本人还有名。它走到哪儿，哪儿的狗就不叫了；它走到哪儿，哪儿的人就突然想起来，家里的鸡好像还没喂。

那天傍晚，天边的云突然一暗。

一阵狂风卷着落叶灌进村子。村口的狗集体闭上了嘴。树上的麻雀，排着队，一只接一只，飞走了。

你放下手里的柴刀，叹了一口气。

你知道，**他**来了。

「砰——！」

你家的柴门飞了出去。它在空中转了三圈，姿态优美，落在隔壁{伴}家的菜地里，砸扁了一颗白菜。

那颗白菜，{伴}家种了一个秋天。

门口站着一个人，把夕阳挡得严严实实。

马三。

他身后，走出来一个圆滚滚的身影。那身影每走一步，地面都要抖一下——主要是他自己在抖。

马小宝。马三的独子，比你大两岁，重你一倍，穿一身绸子，走起路来像一只成了精的糯米团子。他手里，捏着一块桂花糕。

**马三**：（短棍敲着门框，一下，一下，节奏感很好）山——租——

**爹**：（扑通一声跪下）三爷！

**马三**：我还没说完。

**爹**：我先跪着。您慢慢说。

马三愣了一下。显然，他收了这么多年租，头一回碰上这么配合的。

**马三**：……还差一张鹿皮，二十斤肉。入冬前交不上——

他的目光在屋里转了一圈。转过墙角接水的盆，转过灶台上的碗，最后，落在墙上那张缠着牛筋的旧弓上。

**马三**：——那张弓，我就收了。

**爹**：三爷！那是我爹传给我的！

**马三**：你爹传给你，你传给我。（拍了拍你爹的肩膀，语重心长）传承嘛。我懂。

就在这时，马小宝一摇一摆，绕过他爹，走到了你面前。

他把那块桂花糕，举到了你的鼻子底下。

那一刻，时间变慢了。

你看见那块糕上，每一粒桂花都在发光，金灿灿的，像撒了一层碎金子。你闻见那股香味从你的鼻孔钻进去，顺着喉咙往下滑，一路滑到你空了一整天的肚子里，在那里转了一圈，挥了挥手，又走了。

你听见那块桂花糕，在对你说话。

它说：**你配吗？**

**马小宝**：想吃吗？学声狗叫，给你舔一口。
story.en:
The one who collects the rent is Ma San.

Ma San is some distant nephew of Old Master Ma, and he is built like a door. Not *like* a door — he is more of a door than your family's door; your door at least has gaps in it. To get into a room he has to turn sideways, and turned sideways he has to duck, and ducking he has to breathe in.

At his belt he carries a short club bound with iron. In Shi'ao that club is more famous than he is. Wherever it goes, the dogs stop barking; wherever it goes, people suddenly remember they haven't fed the chickens.

That evening, the clouds at the edge of the sky go suddenly dark.

A gust of wind pours into the village, full of dead leaves. The dogs at the gate shut their mouths, all together. The sparrows in the trees line up and fly off, one after another.

You put down your wood-knife and sigh.

You know: **he** has come.

*"BANG —!"*

Your wicker gate flies off. It turns three graceful circles in the air and lands in {伴}'s family's vegetable patch next door, flattening a cabbage.

{伴}'s family spent a whole autumn growing that cabbage.

Someone stands in the doorway, blocking out the sunset completely.

Ma San.

From behind him waddles a round figure. With every step it takes the ground shakes a little — mostly it's the figure itself that's shaking.

Ma Xiaobao. Ma San's only son, two years older than you and twice your weight, dressed all in silk, walking like a rice dumpling that has become a demon. In his hand, a piece of osmanthus cake.

**Ma San:** (rapping the door frame with his club, tap, tap, great sense of rhythm) Moun — tain — rent —

**Father:** (dropping to his knees with a thud) Third Master!

**Ma San:** I'm not finished.

**Father:** I'll kneel first. Take your time.

Ma San is thrown for a moment. Clearly, in all his years of collecting rent, he has never met anyone this cooperative.

**Ma San:** …Still short one deer hide, twenty jin of meat. Not paid before winter —

His eyes make a circuit of the room. Past the basins in the corner catching drips, past the bowls on the stove, and at last they settle on the old bow bound with ox sinew on the wall.

**Ma San:** — and that bow is mine.

**Father:** Third Master! My father handed that down to me!

**Ma San:** Your father handed it to you, you hand it to me. (patting your father's shoulder, earnestly) Heritage. I get it.

Just then Ma Xiaobao waddles round his father and comes up to you.

He holds the osmanthus cake right under your nose.

In that moment, time slows down.

You see every flake of osmanthus on that cake shining, golden, as if sprinkled with gold dust. You smell it: the scent slips in through your nostrils, slides down your throat, all the way into your stomach that's been empty all day, takes a turn around, waves, and leaves.

You hear the osmanthus cake speaking to you.

It says: **Do you deserve me?**

**Ma Xiaobao:** Want some? Bark like a dog and you can lick it.

exits.means: talks back by parroting his words, does not bark and does not hit back

what.zh: 推你撞上灶台，摔碎了家里四只碗里的一只。
what.en: Shoved you into the stove and broke one of your family's four bowls.

story.zh:
**你**：学声狗叫，给你舔一口。

**马小宝**：……什么？

**你**：什么？

**马小宝**：你学不学？

**你**：正在学。

屋里，安静了。

门口不知什么时候围了半个村子的人。{伴}抱着那颗扁了的白菜，肩膀一抽一抽的。

马三的脸，先是红的，然后变紫，然后变黑，然后变成一种你娘后来说叫「**完了**」的颜色。

**马三**：（短棍往地上一跺）**敢戏弄我儿子！**

马小宝回过神来，气得浑身的肉都在抖，冲上来，伸手推了你一把。

你往后倒。

倒下去的那一瞬间，你的脑子里闪过了很多很多东西——你这十二年短暂而贫穷的一生；你爹的膝盖；你娘的手；村口那棵你爬了一百遍的老槐树；还有，灶台上那四只碗。

然后你的后背，撞上了灶台。

「啪。」

一只碗，从灶台边上，缓缓地、缓缓地，飞了出去。

你看着它在半空中翻转。一圈。两圈。夕阳从门口照进来，照在碗沿上，闪了一下光。

你伸出手。

你的指尖，离它只有一寸。

一寸。

一寸，就是一辈子。

「——啪嚓。」

你躺在地上，望着屋顶那个窟窿。一滴雨正好从窟窿里漏下来，不偏不倚，滴在你的眉心。

「……那是我家四只碗里，」你对着屋顶说，「唯一一只，没有缺口的。」

---

马三一挥手，带着马小宝走了。

走之前，马小宝回过头，冲你挤了挤眼睛，当着你的面，把那块桂花糕一口塞进嘴里，腮帮子鼓得像两个包子。

门还在{伴}家的菜地里。

你娘蹲下来，一片一片地捡碗的碎片。

**爹**：他娘……碗碎了，可以再买……

**娘**：拿什么买？

**爹**：……拿……拿我的膝盖？

**娘**：你的膝盖，值几个钱？

**爹**：（认真地想了想）阴天的时候，挺准的。能当个天气预报。

你娘没有笑。

她就那么蹲着，手里捏着一片碗，很久很久，没有动。

你爹也不说话了。他慢慢地蹲下去，挨着你娘，和她一起捡。两个人，一片，一片，捡得很慢很慢。好像捡快了，那只碗，就真的没了。

你躺在地上，看着屋顶那个窟窿。

雨一滴一滴地落在你脸上。凉的。

你忽然，就不想说俏皮话了。

那天夜里，你对着屋顶的窟窿，很小很小声地，说了一句话：

「有一天，我要让我娘，一辈子不用蹲在地上捡东西。」

屋顶没有回答。

只有一滴雨，落进了你娘摆在墙角的第十七个盆里——

叮。

那一夜，你没怎么睡。

隔着一道布帘，你听见爹娘在低声说话。说了很久很久。后来你娘哭了一小会儿。又不哭了。

你躺在炕上，一笔一笔地算账。

这是你娘教你的。你娘说，遇事，先算账。

马小宝比你高一个头，重你一倍——打起来，你输。就算你赢了，门口站着马三，马三手里有棍子——打起来，你爹挨揍。就算你连马三也打赢了——

你想了一下这个画面：十二岁的你，一拳把一扇门打倒在地。

你觉得这个「就算」，有点太远了。

所以今天，你没还手。你只是回了一句嘴。

回嘴，不算还手。这是你给自己定的规矩。

你在黑暗里睁着眼睛，把马小宝推你那一下，马三看那张弓的眼神，那只飞出去的碗，还有你娘停在半空的手——一样一样，记下来。

马三。马小宝。马家老爷。还有马家老爷那个做书吏的远房表侄。

你在心里，一个一个地，骂了一遍：

**你爷爷的。**

**现在打不过。**

你在心里，把这五个字念了一遍。

然后你又念了一遍最后两个字。

**现在。**
story.en:
**You:** Bark like a dog and you can lick it.

**Ma Xiaobao:** …What?

**You:** What?

**Ma Xiaobao:** Are you going to do it or not?

**You:** I'm doing it.

The room goes quiet.

Half the village has gathered at the doorway at some point. {伴} is clutching the flattened cabbage, shoulders shaking.

Ma San's face goes red first, then purple, then black, then a colour your mother would later call "**done for**."

**Ma San:** (stamping his club on the floor) **You dare make a fool of my son!**

Ma Xiaobao comes to his senses, so furious every bit of flesh on him is trembling, charges up and shoves you.

You topple backward.

In the instant you fall, a great many things flash through your head — your twelve short, poor years of life; your father's knee; your mother's hands; the old locust tree at the village gate you've climbed a hundred times; and the four bowls on the stove.

Then your back hits the stove.

*Clack.*

One bowl, from the edge of the stove, slowly, slowly, takes flight.

You watch it turn over in mid-air. Once. Twice. The sunset comes in through the doorway and catches the rim, a single flash.

You reach out.

Your fingertips are one inch from it.

One inch.

One inch is a whole lifetime.

"— *Crash.*"

You lie on the floor, staring up at the hole in the roof. A drop of rain leaks through it and lands, dead centre, right between your eyebrows.

"…That was," you tell the roof, "the only one of our four bowls without a chip in it."

---

Ma San waves a hand and leaves, taking Ma Xiaobao with him.

On the way out Ma Xiaobao looks back, winks at you, and right in front of you stuffs the whole osmanthus cake into his mouth, cheeks bulging like two steamed buns.

The door is still in {伴}'s family's vegetable patch.

Your mother crouches and picks up the pieces of the bowl, one by one.

**Father:** Wife… a broken bowl, we can buy another…

**Mother:** With what?

**Father:** …With… with my knee?

**Mother:** And what is your knee worth?

**Father:** (thinking it over seriously) On cloudy days it's very accurate. It could be a weather forecast.

Your mother doesn't laugh.

She just crouches there, a shard of bowl in her hand, for a long, long time, not moving.

Your father goes quiet too. Slowly he crouches down beside her and picks up the pieces with her. The two of them, one shard, then another, very, very slowly. As if picking faster would make the bowl truly gone.

You lie on the floor, looking at the hole in the roof.

Rain falls on your face, drop by drop. Cold.

All of a sudden, you don't feel like being funny.

That night, to the hole in the roof, very, very quietly, you say one thing:

"One day I'll make it so my mother never has to crouch on the floor picking things up, ever again."

The roof doesn't answer.

Only a drop of rain falls into the seventeenth basin your mother set out in the corner —

*Ting.*

You hardly sleep that night.

Through the cloth curtain you hear your parents talking low. They talk for a long, long time. Then your mother cries for a little while. Then stops.

You lie on the brick bed doing the accounts, one entry at a time.

Your mother taught you that. When something happens, she says, do the accounts first.

Ma Xiaobao is a head taller than you and twice your weight — fight him, you lose. Even if you won, Ma San is standing in the doorway, and Ma San has a club — fight, and your father gets beaten. Even if you beat Ma San too —

You picture it for a moment: twelve-year-old you, felling a door with one punch.

That "even if," you decide, is a bit of a stretch.

So today you didn't hit back. You only talked back.

Talking back isn't hitting back. That's a rule you made for yourself.

Eyes open in the dark, you write it all down, one thing at a time — Ma Xiaobao's shove, the way Ma San looked at the bow, the bowl that flew, and your mother's hand stopped in mid-air.

Ma San. Ma Xiaobao. Old Master Ma. And Old Master Ma's distant nephew, the one who clerks at the county.

In your heart, one by one, you curse every one of them:

**Your grandpa's.**

**Can't win it now.**

You say the words over to yourself once.

Then you say the last one again.

**Now.**

exits.means: hits back, clenches fists, tries to fight Ma Xiaobao

You clench your fists.

Your father is quicker. Still on his knees, he shuffles forward — right in front of you, blocking you completely.

**Father:** Third Master, the child's young, doesn't know any better.

Ma San's club comes down on your father's shoulder. A dull thud.

Your father sways, makes no sound, the smile still on his face — a smile uglier than crying.

**Father:** (to Ma San) What a strong arm you have.

Your fists open, a little at a time.

Ma Xiaobao hasn't had enough fun yet. He charges up and shoves you.

You topple backward.

Ma San waves a hand and leaves, taking Ma Xiaobao with him.

On the way out Ma Xiaobao looks back, winks at you, and right in front of you stuffs the whole osmanthus cake into his mouth, cheeks bulging like two steamed buns.

The door is still in {伴}'s family's vegetable patch.

Your mother crouches and picks up the pieces of the bowl, one by one.

**Father:** Wife… a broken bowl, we can buy another…

**Mother:** With what?

**Father:** …With… with my knee?

**Mother:** And what is your knee worth?

**Father:** (thinking it over seriously) On cloudy days it's very accurate. It could be a weather forecast.

Your mother doesn't laugh.

She just crouches there, a shard of bowl in her hand, for a long, long time, not moving.

Your father goes quiet too. Slowly he crouches down beside her and picks up the pieces with her. The two of them, one shard, then another, very, very slowly. As if picking faster would make the bowl truly gone.

You lie on the floor, looking at the hole in the roof.

Rain falls on your face, drop by drop. Cold.

All of a sudden, you don't feel like being funny.

That night, to the hole in the roof, very, very quietly, you say one thing:

"One day I'll make it so my mother never has to crouch on the floor picking things up, ever again."

The roof doesn't answer.

Only a drop of rain falls into the seventeenth basin your mother set out in the corner —

*Ting.*

You hardly sleep that night.

Through the cloth curtain you hear your parents talking low. They talk for a long, long time. Then your mother cries for a little while. Then stops.

You lie on the brick bed doing the accounts, one entry at a time.

Your mother taught you that. When something happens, she says, do the accounts first.

Ma Xiaobao is a head taller than you and twice your weight — fight him, you lose. Even if you won, Ma San is standing in the doorway, and Ma San has a club — fight, and your father gets beaten. Even if you beat Ma San too —

You picture it for a moment: twelve-year-old you, felling a door with one punch.

That "even if," you decide, is a bit of a stretch.

So you opened your fists. That blow on your father's shoulder cost more than any punch.

Eyes open in the dark, you write it all down, one thing at a time — Ma Xiaobao's shove, the way Ma San looked at the bow, the bowl that flew, and your mother's hand stopped in mid-air.

Ma San. Ma Xiaobao. Old Master Ma. And Old Master Ma's distant nephew, the one who clerks at the county.

In your heart, one by one, you curse every one of them:

**Your grandpa's.**

**Can't win it now.**

You say the words over to yourself once.

Then you say the last one again.

**Now.**
